results.title: Nvidia B200 Price Hits $8.01/Hr as GPU Costs Diverge
results.author: Tom Vance
highlights:
Renting a Nvidia B200 by the hour has no single market price, because Nvidia does not sell it by the GPU-hour and each cloud sets its own rate. Listings in November 2026 reportedly run from $4.11 per GPU-hour, the lowest listed on-demand rate, at Beam Cloud to $16.11 per GPU-hour. Google Cloud listed $16.11 on demand in us-west1 on November 6. Treat any single average, including one quoted from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, as a snapshot to check against provider pages. The B200 is listed as available for rental across multiple cloud providers as of November 6, 2026, and its status is active. It is no longer the only Blackwell option: HGX B300 systems based on Blackwell Ultra became generally available on Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped deployments on October 20, 2026, and Vera Rubin NVL72 is marked early access. Older B200 snapshots, H100 and H200 prices, and any one provider’s rate should not be read as the current market-wide B200 price. Check each provider’s current terms before you commit.

...

The core data point comes from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, which tracks day-to-day cloud rental rates across a basket of providers. In late September 2026, that index put B200 rental pricing at $8.01 per GPU-hour, a 79% climb from where it sat three months earlier. That figure is a market average rather than a price Nvidia publishes or any single provider charges, and a separate October 2026 report from Uvik put B200 median rental pricing at $8.19/GPU-hour across 9 providers, a similar level measured a different way. The same analysis calculated that a B200 now costs 21% more per unit of compute than an H100, a full reversal from June 2026, when a B200 was actually 18% cheaper than an H100 on the same compute-adjusted basis.

...

None of this happens in a vacuum. High-bandwidth memory production is concentrated among a small number of suppliers, and 2026 has been a year of persistent HBM tightness across the entire AI hardware stack. Nvidia’s own next-generation Rubin Ultra platform has reportedly had to trim memory allocation per package because of the same shortage, and cloud providers including Nebius have already raised prices to reflect higher input costs on memory-heavy configurations. When the memory that feeds B200 and H200 packages is scarce and expensive to source, that cost gets passed straight through to the hourly rental rate.

...

The $8.01 index figure is an average, so the price a team actually pays depends on the provider and on how the capacity is billed. In October 2026, Cloud-GPUs tracked B200 availability across 14 providers in 27 countries and listed B200 spot rates at $3.95 to $8.75/GPU-hour, while GPU Economy listed Google Cloud’s B200 spot rate at $1.45/hour. In November 2026, Modal listed B200 at $6.25/GPU-hour, Lambda listed an 8×B200 instance at $6.69/GPU-hour, and Runpod Secure Cloud listed B200 at $7.99/GPU-hour.

Older listings show how wide the spread already was. In February 2025, GPUTracker listed B200 spot pricing at $1.67/hour from Verda. In February 2025, GPUTracker listed B200 on-demand pricing at $3.40/hour from Vast.ai, and it listed Lambda’s B200 on-demand price at $3.99/hour. It also listed GB200 on-demand pricing at $6.50/hour from CoreWeave in February 2025.

Put together, these listings mean that spot, on-demand and whole-instance prices are different products, and a single headline rate hides that. An eight-GPU hyperscaler instance and a single-GPU marketplace listing are not interchangeable, so a budget built on the index average can be wrong in either direction. Before committing to a provider, compare like with like: the same billing model, the same GPU count per instance and the same date. Historical rates should be treated as history rather than as a quote, and a spot price should not be assumed to stay available for a long-running job.

...

Cloud providers themselves are caught in the middle. Neoclouds like CoreWeave, which made HGX B200 instances generally available in May 2025, and Lambda Labs, which built businesses around reselling Nvidia capacity, have to pass through higher acquisition costs or eat margin. Some have already chosen the former: Nebius, one of the higher-profile AI-cloud operators, raised its own pricing in 2026 citing rising memory costs, and it reportedly lifted its B200 on-demand rate from $7.15 to $8.50 per GPU-hour on October 1, 2026, a move and a price level that line up directly with the HBM scarcity driving the B200 and H200 numbers here.

results.title: Lambda Review, Pricing & Alternatives | Saaskly
highlights:
## What it costs

 Prices are in US dollars, VAT not stated, read 22 September 2026. Lambda charges per GPU per hour, and the rate goes up as you take fewer GPUs, which is the opposite of what most buyers expect. One H100 SXM 80 GB costs $4.29 an hour, or $3,132 a month at 730 hours. Take the whole eight-GPU node and the same GPU costs $3.99 an hour, so the node is $31.92 an hour and each GPU works out at $2,913 a month. Two and four GPU configurations sit in between at $4.19 and $4.09. An H100 PCIe is $3.29 an hour. The cheapest GPU on the list is a Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB at $0.69 an hour, about $504 a month, and a GH200 is $2.29. No H200 appears on the public price list at all, despite the pricing page's own marketing copy mentioning it. There is no spot, preemptible or interruptible tier, so there is no cheap way to buy compute you are willing to lose. Reserved pricing for a single on-demand instance is sales only: no rate, no term and no discount figure is published.

 The one published committed option is a 1-Click Cluster, and the arithmetic is counterintuitive. Sixteen H100s cost $6.16 per GPU-hour on a term of two weeks to a year, falling to $5.85 at 64 GPUs and $5.54 at 256. All three are higher than the $3.99 on-demand rate for an eight-GPU node, so a cluster buys InfiniBand and guaranteed capacity rather than a discount. The smallest cluster you can book is 16 GPUs for two weeks, roughly $33,100 paid up front, which puts it out of reach for most small teams. Storage is billed separately and keeps running after the instance has gone: the documentation gives $0.20 per GiB a month as an example and shows the real rate when you create the filesystem, so a 2 TB filesystem left behind costs around $400 a month. Ingress and egress are free and stated as such. On-demand instances bill in one-minute increments and are invoiced weekly in arrears, while clusters bill weekly and are paid in advance. Instances are billed for as long as they are running whether or not they are being used, and no stop-and-keep-the-disk state is documented, so the practical choice is to terminate or keep paying the full rate. The smallest realistic monthly bill for a small team is a Quadro RTX 6000 at $503.70 plus a 500 GB filesystem at about $100, so roughly $604 a month with no transfer charges on top.

...

## Pricing

Minimum commitment: $3,132 ($3,132/mo × 1 seat × 1 month (no commitment)). The least you can spend before walking away; excludes numbers, minutes and add-ons.

### H100 SXM 80 GB, one GPU

$3,132/mo · no commitment

Same price on any term

### Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB, one GPU

results.title: Frontier AI energy economics - Tokens per megawatt-hour
results.author: Mehul Kumar
highlights: At $50 per MWh electricity is 5% of the total; at $120, 11%. A B200 megawatt costs about the same, near $8 million, with 546 GPUs at 1.83 kW of system power each and $45,000 apiece, though each of those chips does several times the work. Facility overhead varies too: Google’s fleet averaged PUE 1.09 in 2025, against the 1.21 assumed here. Renting at assumed on-demand rates of $2.50 to $4 per H100-hour, a range that brackets Lambda’s September 2026 list price of $3.99, would cost $17 to 27 million a year. For context, CoreWeave’s second-quarter 2026 revenue of $2.58 billion comes to about $6.9 million a year per megawatt of the 1.5 GW it had active at the end of June, close to the $7.7 million a year our budget says a megawatt costs to own; it added nearly 500 MW during the quarter, so revenue per megawatt actually in service was higher. Its second-quarter net interest expense of $640 million, annualised, adds roughly $1.7 million per megawatt-year, the financing our budget leaves out. These are company-wide ratios, not H100 rental quotes.

results.title: The weakest version of every AI number is the one someone signed
results.author: Haircut
highlights:
Lambda paid for its grid connection and agreed to be switched down

Lambda’s release gave me three contractual facts to work with. Lambda pays all of its energy costs, it funds the grid infrastructure needed for the site up front, and some of the compute can shift or reduce during peak demand. I still do not have the basic underwriting terms: site megawatts, tariff, credit package, energization date, how much GRDA can cut, how much notice it has to give, or how long a cut can last. Those stay blank.

GRDA had already moved on its side. On 9 September it dedicated a $525m, 426 MW fast-start gas unit to replace a 492 MW coal unit. Nameplate fell by 66 MW, or 13.4%, but the replacement can ramp around a wind-heavy grid. Eighteen days later Lambda showed up with a load designed to ramp the other way when needed. The industrial park has been pitching data centers since at least August 2024, so the sequencing looks deliberate to me.

...

What GRDA needs during the worst hour is pretty different from what a campus calls contracted power. A training job that can sit for six hours and an inference service with a latency promise can both show up as the same number of megawatts in a table. At 6pm on a hot August day they are very different loads. Lambda is paying cash up front for the grid connection and giving GRDA some ability to reduce demand later. I now want both written next to the megawatt number.

...

A month earlier Lambda closed a $926m term loan with unusually clean alignment for GPU ... Lambda also closed a $1bn secured facility from May.

...

Then there is the curtailment clause. If GRDA cuts the site at peak, the economics depend almost entirely on Lambda’s customer contracts. If the jobs can move, Lambda is mostly dealing with scheduling friction. If the customer bought guaranteed throughput, the lost hour can sit with Lambda. Training and guaranteed inference are very different here, and neither Lambda nor GRDA has published enough to tell me the mix.

...

Using one H200 at about 1.42 kW makes the scale pretty obvious. At Oklahoma’s June industrial price of 7.37 cents per kWh, pausing it for an hour saves roughly ten cents of electricity. If the customer stops paying for that hour, Lambda gives up $1.64 of rent on the filed one-year contract reference, or $3.19 on a seller’s current one-year ask. The break-even power price is about $1,157/MWh on the filed rate and $2,250/MWh on the ask. I rechecked the first number because it looked ridiculous. It is still about 16 times what Oklahoma industry paid in June.

Sources: CCIR term curve (26 September print), EIA via YCharts, Oklahoma industrial electricity price, Ornn H200. The 1.42 kW per GPU is my assumption.

From GRDA’s side this is attractive. It gets the site-specific infrastructure funded before its own service spend is stranded, and when the system is tight it has a load that can come down. Lambda takes the scheduling problem, and the GPUs keep ageing whether the jobs run or wait. I am leaving flexible megawatts at face value in the capacity table, but I am not treating them as fully firm until I can see the customer terms behind the curtailment.

GPU prices gave me the same accounting problem in a much easier form because there are actual numbers to compare.

H200 now has four prices, and they disagree on whether it makes money

H200 settled at $4.62 per GPU-hour on the 27th, down 3.3% on the day and 11.5% over seven days. At the same time, CCIR’s 26 September term print moved its systematic one-year H200 price from $3.59 to $3.78. A seller’s one-year ask on the same page is $3.19, and the filed one-year contract reference is $1.64. So I now have four public H200 prices sitting between $1.64 and $4.62.

Day seven had three prices for a GPU. H200 now has four. I held the rest of the ownership model fixed at $39.9k of hardware per GPU, 80% utilization, a 70% one-year residual and the same funding, then changed only the revenue line. One-year economic carry comes out at +23.2% on the systematic ladder, +12.9% on the seller ask and -14.3% on the filed contract. That is a 37.6-point spread from one input. Break-even on those assumptions is about $2.46 an hour. The ladder clears it by $1.32 and the filed contract sits $0.82 below it.

Sources: CCIR term curve (26 September print), Ornn H200. Carry figures use my own hardware, utilization and residual assumptions; the executed $4.62 is a daily price and is not annualized as contract revenue. The $2.46 break-even is my calculation.

Day nine’s test was whether the posted one-year prices would follow spot lower. On the 27th they went the other way. Spot fell again while the systematic ladder rose to $3.78, which mechanically lifted modeled H200 carry from 19.9% to 23.2% on a day the executed market weakened. I read that as a reference-price move. For current underwriting, the $3.19 seller ask is a more useful check and it leaves about half the cushion.

These prices describe different deals, so I do not expect them to converge. The systematic ladder is built from a seller panel. The ask is one seller’s posted number. The filed contract is older, comes from whatever was disclosed, and carries the buyer’s size, credit and support terms with it. I stopped letting one H200 number do every job in the model. Current debt cover uses the signed contract, renewal uses the price a replacement customer could actually get, and recovery uses the hardware resale market.

...

Same utilization, same residual assumption, 3.3 times the purchase price purely from the rent input. CCIR publishes $47,166 on its integrated hardware page and about $33,416 on the B200 chip page, both between those two ceilings.

...

Under the board’s own rules, the carry is correct because it only moves on comparable disclosures. A few rows are starting to look stale anyway. The evidence ledger is identical to the 26th and the newest item is from 24 September. Compute pricing still says ‘firm to higher in PAYG’ after executed H200 fell 11.5% in seven days. Older-GPU residuals still read firm while the H100 resale evidence I have is roughly 46% below posted asks. Behind-the-meter power still reads up, while Oklahoma has now made the utility alternative more explicit and Lambda has shown what a customer has to give up to use it. None of Lambda’s announcement is in the ledger. The macro row still carries the 10-year at 5.18%, versus about 5.17% on Treasury’s curve for the 25th. The full board is below.

...

The next thing I want is the paper that has not been published yet. For Lambda, that is the GRDA service agreement: how many megawatts can be cut, for how long, with what notice and compensation, and whether agreeing to curtailment got the site power sooner. For H200, I want more direct seller asks and I want to see whether they cluster near the $3.78 ladder or the $3.19 ask. For funding, SoftBank’s notes settle on the 29th. After that I am watching the OpenAI tranche and Nebius’s new list prices on 1 October, DDTL 5.0’s hedge date on 14 November, NVIDIA’s $1bn at Nscale in mid-November and Jupiter’s air-permit decision on 23 November.

results.title: Lambda Closes $1 Billion Senior Secured Fixed Rate Financing
results.author: Lambda Media Contact
highlights:
The financing is backed by contracted cash flows from two hyperscale customers, diversifying offtake exposure within a single publicly rated investment-grade GPU debt financing for the first time

SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Lambda, Inc. (“Lambda”), the Superintelligence Cloud, today announced the closing of a $1 billion investment-grade, delayed draw term loan (the “Facility”) marketed to insurance companies and fixed income investors to fund the purchase and development of GPU infrastructure supporting three committed customer deployments with two investment-grade offtakers across multiple data centers.

 The Facility is Lambda’s first U.S. fixed rate financing and its first $1 billion-plus institutional debt financing, expanding the company’s access to institutional credit markets for AI infrastructure financing. The Facility was oversubscribed and received an A (low) rating from Morningstar DBRS and a Baa1 rating from Moody’s. 

 Lambda will use proceeds of the transaction to fund the purchase and development of GPU infrastructure supporting three committed customer deployments with two investment-grade offtakers across multiple data centers. Strong market interest and Lambda’s recent comparable transaction enabled pricing inside the target pricing range of a 6.78% fixed interest rate. 

 The Facility represents Lambda’s second institutional credit facility, following its broadly syndicated loan financing which closed on August 27, 2026, and expands the company’s ability to access institutional capital to support the continued growth of its AI infrastructure. Across its major 2026 financings, Lambda has raised approximately $1 billion in each transaction, establishing a track record of raising debt capital at scale. 

 Facility Highlights 

- $1.008 billion delayed draw term loan 
- A (low) rating from Morningstar DBRS and Baa1 rating from Moody’s 
- 6.78% fixed interest rate on a semi-annual coupon basis 
- Proceeds to fund GPU infrastructure supporting three committed customer deployments with two investment-grade offtakers across multiple data centers 
- Facility final maturity of May 30, 2033, with a fully amortizing repayment profile 
- Secured by the GPU servers and related infrastructure funded by the Facility and the contracted cash flows

results.title: Rental Rates for Older AI Chips Jump 25% as Demand Surges - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: Seo Ji-hye, Kim Ji-young
highlights:
Vessl AI raised its hourly rate for Nvidia H100 graphics processing units by 24.7% starting this month, following a string of price increases by U.S. neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius amid a surge in demand for artificial intelligence computing. Supply has tightened not only for the newest chips but also for older models as demand for high-performance GPUs jumps. Other Korean cloud providers also expect to raise GPU rates depending on supply conditions, raising concerns that higher costs of securing GPUs will weigh on service development at Korean AI companies and on government AI transformation, or AX, projects.

Vessl AI on the 1st raised the hourly rate for H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39, according to AI industry sources on the 21st. The neocloud company counts leading Korean AI firms including Upstage and Motif Technologies among its clients and currently operates several thousand GPUs. It has secured about 7,000 GPUs, most of them leased rather than purchased outright. "It is hard to secure the volume we need for H100s — effectively, the price is whatever the seller names," a Vessl AI official said. "As AI demand grows, the number of customers wanting to use GPUs keeps rising, so a price adjustment was unavoidable." The company plans to expand its GPU fleet to about 10,000 units by the end of the year, but intends to keep adjusting rates flexibly to reflect supply conditions and procurement costs.

Other Korean AI cloud companies, including Elice, have also raised prices recently. In the past, rental rates for older AI GPUs fell when new models arrived, but prices for previous-generation chips are now rising as well. Hourly cloud rental rates for the H100 climbed 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, according to Ornn, an AI compute trading platform. That is about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. Analysts say demand is spilling over to relatively older GPUs because supply of the newest chips cannot keep pace with surging computing demand.

results.title: Lambda and Sharon AI raise $1.356bn in GPU-backed debt priced…
results.author: The Data centers, fiber Desk
highlights:
Lambda's $1bn facility carries a 6.78% coupon and an investment-grade rating; Sharon AI's $365m SPV debt priced at 9.95%.

...

1. Lambda raised $1bn in senior secured fixed-rate financing at 6.78%, an investment-grade delayed-draw term loan marketed to insurance companies and fixed-income investors; Sharon AI, an Australian neocloud, raised $365m of senior secured, GPU-backed special-purpose-vehicle debt at a fixed 9.95%.
2. Lambda says its loan funds GPU cloud infrastructure for three customer deployments it is contracted to support.
3. The spread shows the market paying up for contractual offtake and charging more for everything else, as this publication has argued it would.

The GPU-collateralized debt market printed two reference prices this week, 3.17 percentage points apart. Lambda raised $1bn in senior secured fixed-rate financing at 6.78%, an investment-grade delayed-draw term loan marketed to insurance companies and fixed-income investors; Sharon AI, an Australian neocloud, raised $365m of senior secured, GPU-backed special-purpose-vehicle debt at a fixed 9.95%. Data Center Dynamics, which reported both rounds, puts them together at $1.356bn.

Both facilities are secured against the machines and the cash flows they generate, and both borrowers are spending the proceeds on capacity they have already committed to customers. Lambda says its loan funds GPU cloud infrastructure for three customer deployments it is contracted to support. Sharon's facility is the first in a series the company expects to bring, supporting a plan to deploy 68,000 Nvidia GPUs by the middle of 2027, and it follows an agreement to lease capacity at GreenSquare's Sydney data center, where Sharon intends to install 8,200 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra GPUs.

...

The spread shows the market paying up for contractual offtake and charging more for everything else, as this publication has argued it would. Lambda's coupon is investment grade and went to the buyers who underwrite long-lived contracted assets; Sharon's paper is secured against a named pool of GPUs and their cash flows. Neither deal's tenor is disclosed, which would otherwise sharpen the comparison.

...

GPU-backed lending is growing in popularity but remains a relatively new corner of the credit market, and that newness is why the two coupons carry more information than their sizes. Hardware can be repossessed and carries a defined liquidation value, while the cash flows it produces depend on who has promised to pay for the compute and for how long; two deals this week put a number on the difference: 6.78% for an investment-grade structure against a contracted order book, and 9.95% for an SPV. GPUs also age on a shorter clock than the buildings that house them, a mismatch the credit market is still learning to price.

...

The next marker is the additional Sharon financing the company says it expects to price: a second facility near 9.95% would make that coupon the going rate for a young issuer pledging GPUs, while a lower one would recast it as the cost of a debut. Lambda's next trip to the market, and the coupon it draws, is the other half of the comparison.

results.title: GPU prices surge, on-demand rates increase 53% in 6 ...
results.author: Taylor D.
highlights:
In 2023, if you could get an Nvidia H100 at all, it rented for about $8 an hour. The H100 was the chip everyone wanted for training AI models.

Supply was short, so whoever had them set the price.Then the supply arrived. By October 2024, Eugene Cheah at Latent Space counted seven different resale markets offering H100s for under $2 an hour. He also worked out where the floor was. If an H100 costing about $50,000 rents for less than $1.65 an hour, the provider loses money on it over five years.

So the story most of us took on board was simple. GPUs get cheaper. Wait a quarter and the price drops. Plan your budget around that.

That story stopped being true this year. In early May, Nebius listed the H100 at $2.95 an hour. A round of increases in June took it to $3.85. Yesterday it went to $4.50.

That is roughly 53% more than in May, for a chip that came out in 2022. The newest chip on their list, the B300, went from $7.85 to $9.50.The CPU-only servers went up too. CPU rates rose 25% and memory 41%.

So teams that never touch a GPU are paying more as well. Here is how it works. The on-demand rate is the ceiling.

Nebius says customers who commit to large clusters for several months pay up to 35% less.

Meanwhile, by the company's own account, about 70% of the deals it closed last quarter included prepayments covering 50 to 60% of the cost of building the capacity.

So the big buyers are paying upfront for capacity that does not exist yet. Whatever is left over gets sold by the hour, at whatever price the market will bear.

That means a rising on-demand price is not a premium for some special service. It is what you pay for not having committed early.
